meta.title: AIXTRON SE — Felix Grawert's MOCVD compound-semiconductor deposition franchise through the GaN power, SiC, and micro-LED cycles
meta.abstract: AIXTRON SE (Frankfurt Xetra: AIXA; SDAX index member) is the principal German metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) equipment supplier — its tools deposit the compound-semiconductor epitaxial layers (GaN, SiC, GaAs, InP) that go into power electronics, micro-LED displays, laser diodes, photonics, and RF devices. Headquartered in Herzogenrath near Aachen, Germany. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 has centered on the GaN power electronics inflection (GaN-on-Si for automotive, data-center and consumer power), the SiC power equipment cycle, the still-uncertain micro-LED display thesis, and CEO Felix Grawert's leadership through the post-Schulte transition.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## AIXTRON at a Glance

Four decades after its founding as a spin-off from RWTH Aachen University and the Max Planck Institute, AIXTRON SE had reinvented its revenue mix once already — surviving the LED MOCVD supercycle and its violent unwind — and by 2025 stood positioned for a second structural inflection, this time driven by compound semiconductors in power electronics. The company trades on Frankfurt Xetra as AIXA.DE, a member of the SDAX, and is headquartered in Herzogenrath in the Aachen region, a few kilometres from its academic birthplace. Felix Grawert, President of the Executive Board and sole CEO since Bernd Schulte's retirement at the end of 2023, had built the equipment franchise around two platform generations — the G5 and the G10 — and by 2025 was pivoting its commercial narrative toward AI infrastructure as the next durable demand vector.

## Fiscal 2025 in Brief

Full-year 2025 revenue came in at [€556.6 million](https://compoundsemiconductor.net/article/123615/Aixtron_posts_robust_results_in_a_tough_market) (approximately $615 million at prevailing rates), a 12% contraction from the €633.2 million recorded in 2024. Order intake declined more gently, to €544.3 million from €596.4 million, leaving an equipment backlog of €257.8 million at year-end. EBIT fell to €100.3 million, compressing the operating margin from 21% to 18% — a result that arrived at the top of the company's revised full-year guidance range of 17–19%, and well above the analyst fears that had stalked the stock through mid-year.

| Metric | FY2024 | FY2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | €633.2m | €556.6m | −12% |
| Order intake | €596.4m | €544.3m | −9% |
| EBIT | €131.2m | €100.3m | −24% |
| EBIT margin | ~21% | 18% | −3 pp |
| Gross margin | ~41% | 40% | −1 pp |
| Free cash flow | Negative | €181.9m | — |

The 18% EBIT margin masked a more meaningful shift in product mix. Power electronics — combining GaN and SiC tools — accounted for 57% of system revenue in 2025, with optoelectronics at 23% and LED/micro-LED at 15%. A year earlier, micro-LED and conventional LED had together represented 28% of the mix. The compression was direct: Apple's cancellation of its smartwatch micro-LED programme, reported in early 2024, rippled through AIXTRON's order book and pulled the segment's revenue share nearly in half.

## The Platform Architecture

AIXTRON's revenue is built around two distinct MOCVD tool families. The G10-GaN platform serves the gallium nitride power electronics market — GaN-on-Si and GaN-on-SiC epitaxy for devices used in data centre power supplies, EV onboard chargers, and consumer adapters. Customers include Infineon, Navitas Semiconductor, Power Integrations, Innoscience, and GaN Systems. AIXTRON holds an estimated 71% share of the global GaN MOCVD equipment market, a structural dominance that reflects its first-mover depth in the process chemistry.

The G10-SiC platform is younger and occupies more contested ground. SiC CVD epitaxy for power devices pits AIXTRON against ASM International (which acquired LPE to strengthen its SiC position), Veeco (which purchased Swedish start-up Epiluvac in a deliberate move to enter the market), and a cluster of Chinese domestic equipment makers receiving state backing. AIXTRON's share in SiC CVD is estimated at 33–37%, and the company's stated differentiation centres on the 150mm-to-200mm wafer transition — a process window where it argues the G10-SiC platform offers superior defect density control. By H1 2025, AIXTRON had delivered its 100th G10-SiC system, a volume milestone that signalled commercial traction even as Western SiC end-market demand softened.

The third platform revenue stream — optoelectronics — was effectively dormant as a growth driver through most of 2025 before igniting sharply. The G10-AsP system, which deposits GaAs and InP epitaxy for laser diodes, DFB lasers, and VCSELs, had established itself as the tool of record at leading laser manufacturers by mid-year. Customers such as II-VI/Coherent, Lumentum, Sumitomo Electric, and Mitsubishi Electric draw on the platform for datacom lasers feeding AI data centre optical interconnects.

## The 2026 Inflection

A first-quarter 2026 order surge changed the tenor of the company's year. Q1 2026 order intake reached €171 million — up roughly 30% year-on-year — with optoelectronics comprising more than 65% of that figure. AIXTRON raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance in April from an initial €520 million (±€30 million) to €560 million (±€30 million), and lifted the EBIT margin range to 17–20%.

> "The significantly stronger-than-expected demand from the Optoelectronics sector in the first quarter is a very encouraging development... With our G10-AsP system, we have the tool of record for the next generation of photonic components." — Felix Grawert, April 2026

GaN power, by contrast, was described as "stable but soft" in Q1 2026, while SiC was characterised as "weak" owing to substantial global overcapacity built by Wolfspeed, STMicroelectronics, and Chinese producers over the prior two years. Yet Grawert's forward framing was explicit:

> "We expect that AI data centers can become the largest single application for GaN power semiconductors in the near future."

## What the Dossier Asks

The forward research questions that animate this dossier are tightly bounded. How durable is the GaN power inflection once AI data centre power-delivery architectures shift toward 48V and higher-density rack designs? Can AIXTRON defend or expand its SiC CVD share against ASM/LPE and Veeco as the 200mm transition compresses incumbent advantages? What is the residual value — and timeline — of the micro-LED display thesis now that the Apple Watch programme has lapsed and early-stage AR device orders remain sporadic? How does German two-tier governance — Vorstand under Grawert, Aufsichtsrat above — constrain or enable capital allocation at a company carrying €273 million in net cash by end of Q1 2026? And how does a EUR-reporting, globally-selling equipment company manage the translation exposure as dollar-denominated tool orders reprice against euro manufacturing costs? These are the questions the chapters that follow will attempt to answer.

chapters.title: From 1983 RWTH Aachen spin-off through LED cycles to GaN power and SiC inflection
chapters.body:
## Aachen's Compound-Semiconductor Laboratory, 1983

The company that would become Europe's pre-eminent maker of compound-semiconductor deposition equipment began not in a boardroom but in the laboratories of RWTH Aachen University and the adjacent research networks of the Max Planck Gesellschaft. When researchers there spun out a dedicated metal-organic chemical vapour deposition business in 1983, the commercial logic was modest: universities and advanced device laboratories needed reactor equipment capable of growing III-V semiconductor crystals with atomic-layer precision, and the Aachen group had developed that capability. The founding name reflected its origins — AIX, a shorthand for Aachen's chemical-vapour heritage, appended to the suffix TRON to signal industrial ambition.

Herzogenrath, adjacent to RWTH Aachen, became the company's permanent manufacturing base.

Through the 1980s and into the early 1990s, the business served a niche: research institutes, defence-linked compound-semiconductor fabs, and early optoelectronic device manufacturers buying systems capable of growing gallium arsenide, indium phosphide, and related III-V materials. Revenue was measured in tens of millions of euros and the customer roster was small. The key technological advance of those years was the multi-wafer planetary reactor concept, which allowed simultaneous epitaxial growth across multiple wafers by rotating each wafer around its own axis on a gas-cushion bearing — a design that would underpin every subsequent product generation.

## The LED Decade and Its Aftermath

The transformational event for AIXTRON came from an unexpected direction. As solid-state lighting and consumer displays drove adoption of gallium nitride LEDs through the 2000s, the demand for MOCVD reactors capable of growing GaN on sapphire substrates exploded. Asian device manufacturers — initially in Taiwan, Japan, and South Korea, then in rapidly expanding volume in mainland China — needed precisely the multi-wafer planetary reactors that AIXTRON had spent two decades refining. The company's AIX 2000 and successor systems became standard equipment in LED chip fabs across the region.

Between roughly 2007 and 2012, AIXTRON's revenues scaled sharply, reaching a peak of approximately €700 million in the fiscal year 2011 as Chinese LED manufacturers, backed by provincial government subsidies and aggressive capacity targets, placed equipment orders at a pace the industry had never seen. For a company headquartered in a small German city and employing fewer than two thousand people, the growth was dizzying.

The correction was equally severe. By 2012 and 2013, Chinese LED fabs had built far more capacity than the nascent solid-state lighting market could absorb. New orders collapsed, utilisation rates at customer facilities fell sharply, and AIXTRON's order intake entered a multi-year trough. Revenue declined toward the €150–€200 million range and the company posted losses. The LED boom had made AIXTRON; the LED bust exposed an uncomfortable concentration risk in a single application and a single geography.

The episode left marks on how subsequent management would think about portfolio construction. The dependence on Chinese LED volume customers — firms whose buying behaviour was driven as much by subsidy cycles and local government directives as by genuine equipment demand — proved difficult to forecast and impossible to hedge. A company whose core technology was broadly applicable to multiple compound-semiconductor applications had allowed itself to be defined, for a critical window, almost entirely by one of them.

The vulnerability became acute in 2016 when a consortium led by Fujian Grand Chip Investment Fund, a Chinese state-linked vehicle, proposed an acquisition of AIXTRON. The German federal government intervoked its foreign investment review powers and ultimately withdrew the clearance it had initially granted, blocking the transaction. The episode accelerated a broader German and European reckoning with technology-sector acquisitions by state-linked foreign buyers, and it left AIXTRON operating as an independent company at a moment when it needed a strategic reset.

## Grawert and the Strategic Rebuild, 2017–2023

Felix Grawert arrived at AIXTRON in 2017 from McKinsey, where he had advised technology and industrial clients, and was appointed to the Executive Board — initially sharing leadership with Bernd Schulte, the company's long-serving chief executive and co-architect of its LED-era growth. The pairing placed a strategically-oriented outsider alongside an engineer-executive who had built the operational and manufacturing platform over many years. Grawert was confirmed as President of the Executive Board and Chief Executive Officer in 2018, formally leading the strategic reorientation that had begun to take shape.

The pivot had a clear logic. GaN-on-silicon and GaN-on-SiC power electronics were entering a commercialisation phase after years of laboratory development. The physical properties of gallium nitride — higher breakdown voltage, faster switching speed, and lower on-resistance than silicon — made it attractive for power conversion applications in electric-vehicle onboard chargers, data-centre power supply units, and high-efficiency consumer adapters. SiC power devices served an overlapping but distinct segment, with particular strength in high-voltage traction inverters for electric vehicles and grid-connected power systems. Both application areas required MOCVD epitaxial growth equipment. AIXTRON already had the reactor design competence; the question was whether the commercial markets would develop on a timescale relevant to the company's planning horizon.

The product platform that emerged from this period was the G10 series — a family of large-format multi-wafer planetary reactors optimised for GaN-on-silicon and, subsequently, SiC epitaxy. The G10-GaN and G10-SiC tools represented a deliberate move up the performance and pricing curve, targeting production-scale fabs building capacity for power electronics rather than the lower-margin research and LED markets. The parallel G5 platform continued to serve GaAs, InP, and speciality compound-semiconductor applications including laser diodes for datacom transceivers, VCSELs for 3D-sensing modules, and automotive LiDAR sources.

Schulte, who had anchored AIXTRON's continuity through the LED peak, the trough, and the blocked acquisition, retired from the Executive Board at the end of 2023 after a tenure measured in decades. His departure closed one era and left Grawert as the company's sole executive face — a concentration of strategic authority that the company's German two-tier governance structure, with its Aufsichtsrat supervisory board providing oversight, was designed to accommodate.

## The GaN Power and SiC Inflection, 2023–2025

The years between 2023 and 2025 validated, at least partially, the strategic thesis that Grawert had been constructing since his arrival. G10-GaN system shipments scaled as device manufacturers — ranging from Infineon and STMicroelectronics in Europe to Wolfspeed and Navitas in North America and Innoscience in China — invested in GaN-on-silicon epitaxial capacity. The adoption curve in consumer power adapters, driven by the proliferation of USB Power Delivery and gallium nitride charger designs from brands including Anker and Belkin, had produced a tangible volume pull-through that justified production-scale reactor investment.

Data-centre power conversion added a structurally larger demand vector. The accelerating buildout of AI compute infrastructure placed unprecedented demand on power delivery efficiency, and GaN-based power factor correction and conversion designs offered meaningful efficiency gains that hyperscale operators translated directly into operating-cost reductions at the data-centre level. By the time AIXTRON reported its fiscal 2024 results, revenue had recovered to a range above €600 million — a level that returned the company near its 2011 LED-era peak but on a far more diversified application base and with meaningfully higher average selling prices per system.

SiC entered the revenue mix more slowly, reflecting the longer qualification cycles and the entrenched position of existing SiC epitaxy suppliers in a market that Wolfspeed and others had structured around proprietary process relationships. The G10-SiC platform was commercialised and shipped, but its contribution to total order intake through 2024 remained modest relative to GaN.

The one application that had been expected to contribute materially — and did not — was micro-LED display. The thesis had posited that AIXTRON's MOCVD equipment would be required in volume for the epitaxial growth steps underpinning next-generation micro-LED displays for consumer electronics. Reports emerged in early 2024 that Apple had postponed or cancelled its micro-LED programme for the Apple Watch, a development that removed what had been the most credible near-term demand signal from the display application pipeline. The micro-LED thesis was not abandoned — the physics of micro-LED displays still required compound-semiconductor epitaxy — but its contribution to AIXTRON's planning horizon receded into a longer-dated, more speculative position, leaving GaN power and SiC as the principal growth levers entering 2025 and beyond.

chapters.title: G10-GaN, G10-SiC, photonics MOCVD, broader compound-semi equipment
chapters.body:
## The G10 Platform: AIXTRON's Power Electronics Engine

The G10-GaN reactor sits at the centre of AIXTRON's commercial renaissance in power electronics. Developed as a successor to the G5 platform that had served the LED era, the G10 was optimised for 200-millimetre gallium-nitride-on-silicon production — the substrate combination that made GaN power devices economical enough for automotive and data-centre applications at volume. Where the G5 had been a workhorse of LED epitaxy, the G10 repackaged AIXTRON's close-coupled showerhead reactor architecture for the specific demands of power-device epi: tighter thickness uniformity, precise aluminium-gallium-nitride barrier control, and the thermal management necessary for thick GaN buffers grown atop large-diameter silicon wafers.

The commercial case for the tool converged with a structural shift in power conversion. Automotive on-board chargers migrating from silicon IGBTs to GaN transistors, data-centre rack power-supply units targeting 97-per-cent conversion efficiency, and the proliferation of 100-watt-plus USB-C fast-charger adapters all created simultaneous demand for GaN epitaxial wafers at a scale that strained the industry's installed deposition capacity. Device manufacturers across Asia and Europe competed for G10-GaN reactor delivery slots during the 2022–2024 build cycle.

Order-intake geography confirmed the breadth of adoption. Chinese GaN power device makers, spurred by government-backed semiconductor self-sufficiency programmes, represented a meaningful share of G10-GaN order flow through 2023 and into 2024. The concentration introduced customer-mix risk, but it also validated the platform's positioning as the reference tool for a nascent production ecosystem.

## G10-SiC: Staking a Claim Against CVD Incumbents

The G10-SiC programme represented a deliberate stretch into territory historically dominated by hot-wall chemical vapour deposition equipment suppliers — a different MOCVD-adjacent market where AIXTRON's reactor expertise offered a differentiated entry point rather than incumbency.

Silicon carbide epitaxy for power devices — the growth of thin n- and p-type SiC layers on bulk SiC substrates — had long been served by high-temperature CVD tools from suppliers including LPE and Nuflare, operating at temperatures above 1,500 degrees Celsius in horizontal hot-wall reactors. AIXTRON's proposition with the G10-SiC was that a planetary-reactor MOCVD approach, leveraging the company's accumulated understanding of gas-phase uniformity and rotating-disc hydrodynamics, could deliver competitive epi quality at throughputs and defect levels suited for automotive-grade SiC MOSFETs.

The commercial stakes were substantial. Wolfspeed, STMicroelectronics, Infineon, and a cohort of Chinese SiC makers including SICC and TankeBlue were all constructing SiC epitaxy capacity ahead of anticipated electric-vehicle drivetrain demand in the 2025–2028 window. Even a modest share of the SiC epi-tool market — considerably larger in aggregate capital expenditure than the GaN power segment — would represent a material revenue diversification for a company whose revenue base was roughly EUR 600 million in 2024.

Grawert was measured about the SiC timeline in public communications, acknowledging that displacing established hot-wall CVD tools in a conservative, automotive-qualified supply chain required demonstrating defect density and run-to-run repeatability at production scale, not just in application laboratories. The G10-SiC entered early customer qualification cycles during 2023 and 2024, with commercial shipments tracking behind the GaN platform's ramp but accumulating process data that management described as encouraging.

| Platform | Substrate | Primary End Markets | Competitive Landscape | Status (as of 2024) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G10-GaN | GaN-on-Si, GaN-on-SiC | Auto OBC, data centre PSU, fast charge | Veeco EPIK 868, in-house epi | Commercial ramp |
| G10-SiC | SiC-on-SiC | EV drivetrain inverters, industrial | LPE, Nuflare hot-wall CVD | Early qualification |
| G5+ photonics | GaAs, InP | Datacom lasers, VCSELs, LiDAR | Veeco K475i, Thomas Swan | Mature/stable |

## Photonics MOCVD: The Quiet Annuity

While the G10 power platforms attracted the bulk of investor attention, AIXTRON's photonics MOCVD franchise continued to generate steady equipment orders and aftermarket revenue from a geographically diversified customer base that had been constructing datacom and sensing capacity with G5-series tools for more than a decade.

The photonics segment spans three primary application clusters. Datacom transceivers — the edge-emitting laser diodes and electroabsorption-modulated lasers that carry 400G and 800G optical traffic inside hyperscale data centres — are grown on gallium arsenide and indium phosphide substrates in AIXTRON reactors operated by fabs aligned with II-VI/Coherent, Lumentum, and Sumitomo Electric. Automotive LiDAR brought a second demand vector: pulsed 905-nanometre edge-emitting lasers for time-of-flight ranging systems, where AIXTRON's GaAs epi tools were already qualified in the supply chains of Tier-1 automotive laser suppliers. VCSELs for consumer 3D sensing — the structured-light modules behind smartphone face-unlock and gesture-recognition systems — constituted a third, more volatile stream sensitive to platform upgrade cycles at handset OEMs.

The photonics book was not a growth story in the 2022–2025 period; it was a durability story. Datacom laser capacity builds tracked data-centre construction with a lag, and the VCSEL market oscillated with consumer electronics cycles. But the installed base of AIXTRON photonics reactors in customer fabs — each requiring periodic process-kit replacement, spare-part provisioning, and calibration services — generated recurring aftermarket revenue with margins structurally above the equipment sale. AIXTRON's services and spare-parts line, consolidated within its aftermarket reporting, provided a partial hedge against the lumpiness of new-tool orders across all product lines.

## Micro-LED: The Thesis Under Stress

No segment illustrated the asymmetry between thesis and execution more sharply than micro-LED display epitaxy. The micro-LED display thesis — once projected as a transformational MOCVD demand driver — suffered a significant setback in early 2024 when Apple reportedly cancelled or deferred its Apple Watch micro-LED programme. Display panel makers retrenched pilot-scale capacity orders; the multi-hundred-million-euro capacity wave anticipated for 2024–2025 did not materialise.

Grawert acknowledged the deceleration without abandoning the long-term thesis. The segment, he noted, remained technically compelling; the question was timing, not direction. The practical consequence for AIXTRON's medium-term revenue profile was a more concentrated dependence on power electronics — GaN power and, progressively, SiC — to sustain the revenue base that had been partially underwritten by micro-LED expectations.

## Aftermarket, Services, and the Recurring Revenue Layer

Across all tool families, AIXTRON's aftermarket and services business provided ballast against the capital-equipment cycle. The installed base of G5 and G10 reactors in customer fabs required a steady flow of process kits — susceptors, liners, inlet components — that degraded with use and required periodic replacement to maintain epi quality. Extended service agreements, remote diagnostics, and process-optimisation consulting added revenue streams that were structurally less volatile than equipment orders.

AIXTRON did not provide granular aftermarket-revenue disclosure in the format common among US-listed equipment peers such as Applied Materials or Lam Research, but management commentary through 2023 and 2024 indicated that services and spares represented a meaningful and growing share of total revenue as the installed GaN power base expanded. Each G10-GaN tool shipped to a customer fab represented a years-long service relationship; at the volume of G10 deployments accumulated through the 2022–2024 ramp, the compounding annuity of process-kit consumption was becoming a non-trivial revenue contributor that partially smoothed the lumpy new-equipment order book.

The aggregate picture by the frozen snapshot date in May 2026 was of a company whose product architecture had been substantially repositioned — from LED MOCVD toward GaN power, SiC power, and photonics — with micro-LED as a residual optionality rather than a near-term volume driver. The G10-GaN platform had achieved commercial scale; the G10-SiC was in qualification; photonics tools were a stable annuity; and micro-LED remained the chapter whose conclusion the industry had not yet written.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, order intake cyclicality, EBIT margin progression, capital allocation
chapters.body:
The four fiscal years from 2022 through 2025 trace the full arc of a compound-semiconductor capital-equipment cycle: the demand surge that carried AIXTRON from mid-tier profitability to its best-ever results, the plateau, and the controlled compression that followed as GaN power adoption paused and micro-LED display orders failed to materialise. Read in sequence, the numbers form a precise record of both the franchise's earnings power and the structural risks that attend a concentrated, capital-equipment business model exposed to the idiosyncratic buildout timelines of a handful of device chipmakers.

## The Revenue Surge and Its Arithmetic

The fiscal-year pivot came in 2023. After posting revenue of €463.2m in FY2022—itself a respectable 8 per cent gain over the prior year—AIXTRON booked €629.9m in FY2023, a 36 per cent step-change that ranked as the company's strongest annual revenue growth in more than a decade. The catalyst was multifaceted: volume shipments from the G10-GaN platform ramp gathered pace as Infineon, STMicroelectronics, Navitas Semiconductor, and Chinese power-device fabs accelerated GaN-on-Si and GaN-on-SiC capacity expansion; the SiC power epitaxy tool portfolio contributed an incremental stream of orders from Wolfspeed and European tier-one device makers; and optoelectronics deliveries—laser-diode and VCSEL tools for datacom and 3D-sensing—maintained a steady underlying contribution. FY2024 came in almost exactly flat at €633.2m—an increase of less than 1 per cent—revealing that the surge had run its initial course. Revenue plateaued as a handful of large customers digested equipment already received, even as the next wave of demand orders began to rebuild. The picture for FY2025 was more difficult: revenue contracted 12 per cent to €556.6m, the largest single-year decline since the post-LED-bubble correction of 2012–2013, as soft GaN power orders in Asia combined with USD headwinds and the absence of any material micro-LED display business to produce a year in which AIXTRON outperformed only on the cash line.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (€m) | YoY Change | EBIT (€m) | EBIT Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | 463.2 | +8% | 104.7 | 22.6% |
| FY2023 | 629.9 | +36% | 156.8 | 24.9% |
| FY2024 | 633.2 | +1% | 131.2 | 20.7% |
| FY2025 | 556.6 | −12% | 100.3 | 18.0% |

*Sources: [AIXTRON Annual Report 2023](https://www.aixtron.com/en/investors); [AIXTRON FY2024 results press release](https://www.finanzwire.com/press-release/aixtron-well-on-track-in-a-challenging-market-environment-UgcGf0OTr0e); [AIXTRON FY2025 results press release](https://www.webdisclosure.com/press-release/aixtron-se-etr-aixa-aixtron-with-robust-results-in-a-soft-market-environment-yyvmiE66gVE)*

## Order Intake Cyclicality and Backlog Dynamics

For a company whose revenues are delivered with a lag of six to eighteen months after booking, order intake and equipment backlog are the forward-facing vital signs. The FY2022 order intake of €585.9m—18 per cent above the prior year and the second-highest annual figure in AIXTRON's history at the time—seeded the FY2023 revenue surge. The FY2023 order intake of €640.7m, a further 9 per cent gain, signalled that FY2024 revenue would hold: it did, exactly. The deceleration that began in the second half of 2023 then manifested in the order line with a one-cycle lag. FY2024 order intake fell 7 per cent to €596.4m; FY2025 declined a further 9 per cent to €544.3m. Equipment order backlog—the unconverted portion of booked orders—peaked at €353.7m at the end of FY2023 and had eroded to €257.8m by end-FY2025, a 27 per cent drawdown over two years.

| Fiscal Year | Order Intake (€m) | Equipment Backlog (€m) |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | 585.9 | 351.8 |
| FY2023 | 640.7 | 353.7 |
| FY2024 | 596.4 | 289.3 |
| FY2025 | 544.3 | 257.8 |

The composition of the order book shifted substantially during this period. Asia—principally China—contributed a disproportionate share of the FY2022–FY2023 surge as domestic GaN power-device fabs (Innoscience, GaN Systems affiliates, and multiple unnamed entrants) competed to scale capacity. By 2024 that Chinese ordering wave had largely exhausted its first-cycle appetite, and European and South Korean customers were not yet sufficient to replace the volume. Q4 2024 order intake of €157.0m fell 23 per cent against the same period a year earlier; Q4 2025's partial recovery to €169.6m, up 8 per cent, provided the first concrete inflection signal since the downturn began.

## EBIT Margin Progression and Management's Implicit Targets

AIXTRON's EBIT margin trajectory across the four-year window illustrates the leverage—both positive and negative—inherent in a business with high operating costs and relatively sticky R&D expenditure. At the FY2022 EBIT margin of 22.6 per cent, the company already exceeded its publicly communicated guidance band of 20–23 per cent. The FY2023 result of 24.9 per cent sat at the lower end of a mid-year-upgraded guidance range of 25–27 per cent, reflecting a mix effect as volume pulled ahead of realised product-margin improvement. Management has not published a formally labelled "mid-cycle" or "through-cycle" EBIT margin target in the manner of, say, an industrial conglomerate issuing a Capital Markets Day framework; the closest functional equivalent is the 25 per cent level demonstrated in FY2023, which analysts and investors have treated as the proxy peak-cycle target.

The FY2024 compression from 24.9 to 20.7 per cent was caused by three concurrent pressures: unfavourable product mix as a higher proportion of revenue derived from lower-margin repeat orders rather than new-platform tool sales; a step-up in R&D expenditure to €91.4m (14.4 per cent of revenue) as the next-generation Hyperion 300mm GaN platform advanced toward commercialisation; and the first meaningful FX headwind as the US dollar softened relative to the euro. FY2024 initial guidance had targeted 24–26 per cent; the actual outcome of 20.7 per cent represented a significant miss. In the FY2024 results call, CFO Dr. Christian Danninger acknowledged that 2025 would be focused on "strengthening profitability and rebuilding a strong cash position."

The FY2025 EBIT margin of 18.0 per cent, landing at the midpoint of a final revised guidance range of 17–19 per cent, represented the lowest margin since the pre-GaN-power era. Grawert was characteristically measured about the near-term context:

> "In 2025 AIXTRON has performed well in a challenging market environment. We efficiently adjusted our capacity and significantly increased our free cash flow by over EUR 250 million."

The 2026 guidance issued in February 2026—subsequently raised in April 2026 to 17–20 per cent EBIT margin on revenue guidance of €560–620m—signalled that management regarded FY2025 as a trough rather than a reset, with the optoelectronics cycle, particularly AI-driven datacom laser tools, positioned as the primary recovery driver.

## R&D Intensity and the Investment Cycle

One of the more instructive features of the FY2022–FY2025 data is the deliberate decision to maintain, and indeed accelerate, research and development expenditure through the revenue downturn. R&D climbed from €57.7m in FY2022 (12.5 per cent of revenue) to €91.4m in FY2024 (14.4 per cent), before stepping back slightly to €81.1m in FY2025 (14.6 per cent on the lower revenue base). The FY2024 R&D peak coincided with simultaneous development programmes across the G10 tool family completion, early-stage Hyperion platform engineering, and SiC tool qualification work. This cycle of investment-before-revenue is structurally embedded in AIXTRON's model: platform transitions—from G5 to G10, from 150mm to 200mm substrate compatibility, from 200mm to 300mm GaN—require multi-year R&D commitments before any tool sale materialises. The consequence for the margin line is an unavoidable earnings dilution during transition periods that a shorter-cycle business would not exhibit.

## Dividends, Buybacks, and Cash Allocation

The dividend history across the four years traces an arc that closely mirrors the net-income trajectory, with one sharp episode of policy recalibration. AIXTRON paid €0.31 per share for FY2022 and raised that to €0.40 for FY2023, the highest absolute dividend in the company's modern history and a clear signal that management believed the earnings upgrade was durable. The abruptness of the reversal made an impression: the FY2024 dividend was cut to €0.15 per share—a 62.5 per cent reduction—directly reflecting the net profit decline from approximately €145m in FY2023 to €106.2m in FY2024. The FY2025 dividend was held at €0.15, consistent with a roughly 17–20 per cent payout ratio on FY2025 net income of €85.3m. The payout ratio has therefore normalised to a conservative level, prioritising balance-sheet liquidity over shareholder distribution at a moment when the investment cycle for Hyperion and for the €40m Malaysia manufacturing facility (production readiness targeted for mid-2027) competes for capital allocation.

No active share buyback programme was in operation during FY2022–FY2024. At the May 2025 Annual General Meeting, shareholders authorised management to repurchase and cancel treasury shares, but no specific programme size or execution timeline had been disclosed by the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026. The authorisation exists as an option, not a commitment.

## Free Cash Flow and Balance Sheet Reconstruction

The free cash flow record over the period tells a more volatile story than the income statement alone suggests. FY2022 produced a modest free cash flow of €7.7m despite strong profitability, as the working capital cycle absorbed the order-intake surge in advance inventory. FY2023's €629.9m revenue year generated negative free cash flow of €109.7m—an apparent paradox explained by a combination of heavy CapEx associated with the Aachen innovation centre expansion and a substantial build in finished-goods inventory as production ramped ahead of deliveries. FY2024 produced a further negative €72.4m in free cash flow, compressing cash and equivalents to €64.6m at year-end, AIXTRON's lowest liquid-asset balance in the cycle. The FY2025 reversal was dramatic: operating cash flow of €208.4m and free cash flow of €181.9m rebuilt the cash line to €224.6m by year-end, a €160m recovery driven by inventory drawdown, disciplined CapEx restraint, and the structural back-loading of customer prepayments into the second half of the year.

## FX Translation and the EUR/USD Sensitivity

AIXTRON reports in euros but generates a material portion of revenue in US dollars from Asian customers and through USD-denominated contracts. The company typically communicates an annual budget exchange-rate assumption in its guidance: FY2024 was budgeted at 1.15 USD/EUR; FY2025 initial guidance assumed 1.10 (implying a stronger dollar). When the actual rate drifted toward 1.15 during 2025, management flagged in the October 2025 guidance revision that the FX shift alone accounted for approximately one percentage point of the gross-margin reduction and one percentage point of the EBIT-margin reduction in the full-year result. The FY2026 budget rate of 1.20 USD/EUR—reflecting a weaker dollar assumption relative to the FY2025 starting point—embeds another potential headwind. As a structural matter, a sustained move from 1.10 to 1.20 compresses AIXTRON's reported EBIT margin by roughly one percentage point on a through-cycle basis, all else equal, with no operating offset available absent renegotiation of USD contracts or further euro-zone cost reduction. The FX exposure is asymmetric in its P&L impact: revenue translates lower in euro terms while the cost base—predominantly labour and procurement in Germany—remains largely euro-fixed.

chapters.title: Multi-year trajectory through GaN inflection, SiC ramp, and micro-LED reset
chapters.body:
## The Power Electronics Inflection: FY2022

AIXTRON arrived at fiscal 2022 carrying a compound-semiconductor order book reshaped by a decade of structural transition. The LED MOCVD wave had largely passed. In its place, a quieter but more durable current had begun running through demand for gallium nitride: not the blue-LED chips that once lit smartphone screens, but power transistors switching electrical current in electric-vehicle onboard chargers, data-centre power supplies, and consumer fast chargers operating at voltages where GaN's switching speed and lower conduction losses outperformed silicon.

Full-year 2022 revenue reached approximately €441 million, a meaningful step from prior years, as customers converted equipment reservations into purchase orders. Order intake ran ahead of revenue recognition, building a backlog that management described as giving the company "good visibility" into 2023. Felix Grawert, who had been repositioning AIXTRON's product roadmap since taking the CEO role in 2018, described GaN power adoption on earnings calls as transitioning from an early-adopter technology to a "structural" demand driver — one that would persist across multiple customer-capital-expenditure cycles rather than collapsing into a single-wave event of the kind that had defined the LED era.

The geographic composition of that demand told a story about where the GaN power supply chain was consolidating most rapidly. Chinese power-device manufacturers, building out capacity to serve the domestic EV and fast-charging markets, accounted for a disproportionately large share of equipment orders. Renminbi translation into reporting euros added a layer of FX exposure that management flagged but characterised as manageable given the multi-year nature of equipment purchase decisions; order bookings in China were typically quoted in US dollars, partly insulating headline order intake from CNY moves while creating a second translation step when USD revenue was converted to EUR at recognition. This concentration would prove both an accelerant and, in later quarters, a source of volatility.

---

## Record Revenue, Peaking Orders: FY2023

Fiscal 2023 represented the financial apex of AIXTRON's post-LED reconstruction. Revenue rose to approximately €629 million as the company converted its strengthened backlog into shipped tools, and operating margins expanded to levels that reflected the leverage inherent in a capital-equipment franchise with high fixed-cost absorption. EBIT margins pushed into the high-twenties percent range — outperforming the guidance corridor management had issued at the start of the year, a pattern that had become familiar as GaN power demand ran hotter than mid-cycle estimates implied.

Yet even as revenue moved through its record corridor, order intake was already signalling a different trajectory. Customers who had placed reservations in 2021 and 2022 had received their tools and were now in the qualification-and-ramp phase, not the procurement phase. Order intake declined from its 2022 peaks, and Grawert framed this normalisation in the second half of the year not as a demand problem but as an expected digestion period characteristic of the compound-semiconductor equipment cycle.

The micro-LED display thesis moved toward a more cautious register during 2023 as Apple's reported programme faced internal reviews.

---

## The SiC Adjacency

AIXTRON's G10-SiC reactor family addressed the 650-volt-and-above power market — principally EV traction inverters — where SiC's wider bandgap outperforms GaN.

SiC orders provided a counterweight to the China-heavy GaN composition: European and North American automotive customers purchased tools on capex cycles tied to OEM launch timelines.

---

## Revenue Softening and Micro-LED Reset: FY2024

Fiscal 2024 confirmed the cyclical correction that order-intake trends had foreshadowed. Revenue ran in the vicinity of the €600 million range, reflecting lower backlog conversion from a softer 2023 order intake. The margin profile compressed from peak levels as fixed-cost absorption declined. AIXTRON's capital-light model — tool design and final assembly in Germany, components sourced globally — meant that the company maintained profitability through the trough, a structural advantage over the post-2012 LED collapse period when revenue fell by roughly two-thirds and operating losses accumulated for several years. The comparison underscored how substantially the business mix had improved: the power-electronics customer base carried longer replacement cycles and more durable qualification barriers than the commodity LED producers who had driven the earlier cycle.

The most significant narrative shift of 2024 was the effective reset of near-term micro-LED display expectations. Apple's reported deferral of its micro-LED wearable programme removed a speculative near-term catalyst.

GaN power continued to generate recurring tool orders, but velocity had moderated from the Chinese-driven surge of 2022–2023. The deceleration partly reflected customer-fab utilisation: tools purchased at peak had not yet been fully loaded with production volume, reducing urgency for additional capacity additions. Dollar strength in parts of the year added a modest tailwind to USD-denominated order values when translated to euros for reported order intake, but provided limited buffer against the underlying volume decline. Grawert noted that GaN power adoption in non-Chinese markets — European automotive-adjacent applications and North American data-centre power conversion — was accelerating on a longer but more structurally stable adoption curve, providing a floor even as Chinese order cadence normalised.

---

## FY2025: Recovery Trajectory and Structural Question

Entering fiscal 2025, AIXTRON management guided for revenue recovery, underpinned by a SiC order pipeline that had strengthened as European automotive SiC fab programmes moved from planning into equipment procurement. The GaN power market was showing early signs of re-engagement from Chinese customers that had completed device qualifications and were extending capacity for the next wave of EV and fast-charging designs. Order intake began recovering, and management pointed to design-win momentum at power-IC customers across multiple geographies as a leading indicator of tool orders twelve to eighteen months forward.

The micro-LED thesis remained live but distant. The earliest plausible commercial re-entry point for a large-programme tool order had shifted to the latter half of the decade, making display-related equipment revenue a 2027–2028 event at best rather than a near-term catalyst. Grawert maintained that AIXTRON's MOCVD platform held incumbent technology status for whatever micro-LED production ramp eventually arrived, and that ongoing development-tool shipments to display-research customers were preserving both process knowledge and customer relationships through the delay.

For the multi-year earnings story, the structural question had clarified into a single frame: could the SiC ramp grow fast enough — and the GaN power cycle recover durably enough — to more than offset the residual LED MOCVD revenue decline and the deferred micro-LED upside, while sustaining the margin profile that had made AIXTRON's reconstituted compound-semiconductor franchise so much more attractive than its LED-era predecessor. By the close of the frozen-window period, the G5 and G10 Planetary Reactor families were the incumbent tools of record for the two largest next-generation power markets in the global electrification build-out. Whether that incumbency was monetised in a tight two-year window or a stretched four-year cycle remained, as it has throughout AIXTRON's history, the irreducible variable in the investment case.

chapters.title: Felix Grawert, Christian Danninger, Executive Board, Supervisory Board
chapters.body:
AIXTRON's institutional character — designing tools for adoption curves not yet visible — shaped the type of manager who eventually rose to lead it.

## Felix Grawert: An Engineer Trained on Three Continents

Felix Grawert arrived at AIXTRON in August 2017 from a career that had moved through academia, strategy consulting, and industrial product management in an arc that was unusual for a German Mittelstand equipment company. Born in Kiel in 1975, he earned a Diplom-Ingenieur in electrical engineering from the Universität Karlsruhe before crossing the Atlantic: a Master of Science from Georgia Tech, followed by a doctorate in electrical engineering and computer science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, completed in 2005. The MIT PhD was not honorary ballast — it centred on power conversion and semiconductor device physics, the technical substrate on which AIXTRON's GaN and SiC equipment ambitions would later rest.

From 2005 to 2013, Grawert worked as a consultant at McKinsey & Company in Munich, eventually reaching Associate Principal. His sector focus was semiconductors, high technology, and automotive — a triangulation that would prove directly applicable when GaN-on-silicon power electronics began displacing silicon MOSFETs in automotive on-board chargers and data-centre power conversion. He left McKinsey in 2013 for Infineon Technologies, where he served until 2017 as Head of Product Line High Voltage Conversion in Munich and Villach, overseeing the commercial execution of exactly the device category that AIXTRON's G10-GaN platform was designed to enable. When the AIXTRON Supervisory Board went looking for a board-level candidate who combined deep technical grounding in power semiconductors with commercial and strategic discipline, Grawert was an identifiable profile.

He joined the Executive Board in August 2017 alongside co-President Bernd Schulte. For the first three and a half years, the two men ran the company as a diarchy — Grawert taking responsibility for sales, marketing, customer relations, and R&D, Schulte managing operations and manufacturing. [AIXTRON IR](https://www.aixtron.com/en/company/management/executive-board)

## The Schulte Transition and the End of a Multi-Decade Tenure

Schulte's transition began in 2021 when Grawert assumed the Executive Board chairmanship. Schulte's full retirement came at the end of 2023 after navigating the LED equipment cycle's boom, post-boom correction, and diversification into power electronics and photonics.

## Christian Danninger: The Austrian CFO

Dr. Christian Danninger joined as Chief Financial Officer and Executive Board member in May 2021, filling the finance seat that had not previously existed as a standalone Vorstand position. Born in 1979 in Gmunden, Austria, Danninger brought an unusual credential set for a semiconductor equipment company: a doctorate in law from Johannes Kepler University in Linz, supplemented by dual master's degrees in law and business administration. His career had been built in industrial capital-equipment businesses — fifteen years between 2005 and 2021 split across the ENGEL Group, the Austrian plastics-injection-machinery maker, and PUTZMEISTER Holding, the German concrete-pump manufacturer where he had served as CFO from 2017. The profile — a trained lawyer-turned-capital-equipment CFO, comfortable with export-heavy manufacturing businesses and complex international customer financing — suited AIXTRON's profile as a EUR-reporting company selling long-cycle capital equipment globally. Danninger's contract runs to April 2029. [AIXTRON IR](https://www.aixtron.com/en/company/management/executive-board)

## The Linck Interlude and a Lean Two-Person Board

The third Executive Board member appointed in 2021, Dr. Jochen Linck, served as Chief Operating Officer with responsibility for R&D and operations — procurement, manufacturing, logistics, quality, and IT. Linck's departure in September 2023, which the company disclosed in May of that year as a decision not to renew his contract for personal reasons, reduced the Vorstand back to two members. Rather than appointing a successor to the COO seat, AIXTRON created an internal Executive Committee — a layer of senior vice presidents covering the former COO portfolio — that reports directly to Grawert and Danninger. The structure has been characterised internally as a deliberate move toward operating flexibility, concentrating formal accountability at the top while distributing functional depth below board level. [AIXTRON press release, May 2023](https://www.aixtron.com/en/press/press-releases/AIXTRON%20introduces%20new%20Executive%20Committee%20/%20Current%20COO%20Jochen%20Linck%20not%20to%20renew%20his%20contract%20due%20to%20personal%20reasons%20/%20New%20Executive%20Committee%20will%20support%20CEO%20and%20CFO_n2443)

The Supervisory Board's decision in September 2024 to extend Grawert's contract by a further five years — through 13 August 2030 — reflected a verdict on the first three years of his sole tenure. Then-chairman Kim Schindelhauer described the extension in explicit strategic terms: "With Dr Grawert, Aixtron made significant progress in the equipment technology for power electronics." Grawert, in his own statement, kept the language operational: "I am very excited to continue my work at Aixtron and further shape the future." [Compound Semiconductor, September 2024](https://compoundsemiconductor.net/article/120135/Aixtron_extends_CEOand_s_contract)

## Grawert's Strategic Voice

On earnings calls, Grawert tends toward declarative technical-commercial framing rather than promotional tone. The vocabulary of the GaN power thesis — 800-volt architectures, data-centre power-conversion density, the timing of automotive adoption curves — is handled with the precision of someone who ran a power-semiconductor product line, not a generalist CEO who acquired the terminology from investor-relations briefing books. Presenting full-year 2025 results in early 2026 — a year in which revenue fell 12 percent year-on-year to €556.6m and EBIT compressed to €100.3m — he did not attempt to obscure the cyclical softness, but framed the forward thesis clearly:

> "In 2026, optical data communication for AI applications and GaN power will be the main source of revenue. We expect that AI data centers can become the largest single application for GaN power semiconductors in the near future."

During the Q3 2025 call, with revenue already running 23 percent below the prior-year quarter, the acknowledgement was equally direct: "The demand upturn has not yet materialized in Q3/2025." He accompanied that admission with a structural claim: "medium- and long-term growth drivers, e.g. with the introduction of new 800V architectures for AI data centers using both SiC and GaN, remain intact." Whether the cycle has turned by the frozen snapshot date of May 2026 is addressed in the financials chapter; the point here is that Grawert operates with a publicly stated conviction about the end-market trajectory that he has not walked back through the downcycle.

## The Supervisory Board: Industry Credentials Rebuilt Around Semiconductors

Germany's two-tier governance model places the Aufsichtsrat — Supervisory Board — in a constitutionally distinct oversight role from the operating Vorstand. AIXTRON's six-member Supervisory Board, as constituted by the 2025 annual general meeting, has been substantially refreshed since the post-LED-cycle restructuring years.

The most consequential recent change was the election of Alexander Everke as chairman following Kim Schindelhauer's resignation at the 2025 AGM. Everke, who served as CEO of ams-OSRAM AG from 2016 until handing over to Aldo Kamper in early 2023, had grown that company from approximately €500m in annual revenue to roughly €5bn, principally through the acquisition of OSRAM and a strategic pivot toward optical sensing and automotive photonics. His sector biography — Siemens, Infineon, NXP, ams-OSRAM — maps almost directly onto AIXTRON's customer base and growth markets. He chairs both the Nomination and Capital Market committees. [Semiconductor Today, February 2025](https://www.semiconductor-today.com/news_items/2025/feb/aixtron-270225.shtml)

Deputy chairman Frits van Hout, on the board since 2019, brings a complementary perspective: a career that included executive roles at ASML, the Dutch lithography incumbent whose capital-equipment business model and customer-concentration dynamics are structurally familiar to AIXTRON's situation, albeit at a different scale. Van Hout chairs the Remuneration Committee.

The remaining four members span audit, technology operations, and capital-markets expertise. Ingo Bank — CFO of City Football Group and formerly CFO of ams-OSRAM, OSRAM Licht, and Philips — joined in 2025 alongside Everke, deepening the semiconductor-adjacent financial oversight on the board. Dr. Stefan Traeger, chairman of JENOPTIK AG's Vorstand since May 2022, brought optical and photonics industrial perspective. Karen Florschütz, executive vice president at Airbus Defence and Space with prior Siemens operations background, has served since 2024. Prof. Dr. Anna Weber of Heilbronn University chairs the Audit Committee and also sits on the Supervisory Board of Wacker Chemie AG, a Munich-listed specialty-chemicals producer with meaningful semiconductor materials exposure.

| Member | Role | Board since | Background anchor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alexander Everke | Chairman | 2025 | CEO ams-OSRAM, Infineon, NXP |
| Frits van Hout | Deputy Chairman | 2019 | ASML executive, Oxford MA |
| Ingo Bank | Member | 2025 | CFO ams-OSRAM / OSRAM / Philips |
| Karen Florschütz | Member | 2024 | EVP Airbus Defence and Space; Siemens |
| Dr. Stefan Traeger | Member | 2022 | Chairman, JENOPTIK AG Vorstand |
| Prof. Dr. Anna Weber | Member (Audit chair) | 2019 | Heilbronn University; Wacker Chemie |

The concentration of ams-OSRAM alumni — Everke and Bank both served there, as CFO and CEO respectively — at the top of the Supervisory Board in 2025 was the most visible signal of where the board believed AIXTRON's strategic reference points lay: not in legacy LED equipment or generic industrial capital equipment, but in the compound-semiconductor photonics and power-electronics complex that connects MOCVD deposition to AI infrastructure, automotive electrification, and optical datacom. Whether that strategic alignment translates into order-book execution over the remainder of the decade is the question Grawert and Danninger are contracted to answer.

chapters.title: Power, photonics, and display device-maker customers plus the Herzogenrath manufacturing footprint
chapters.body:
AIXTRON's customers sorted into four clusters: GaN power electronics (the core), SiC power devices (contested), photonics (steady), and micro-LED display (thesis unconfirmed).

## GaN Power Electronics: The Core Customer Bloc

The anchoring customers for AIXTRON's G5+ and G10-GaN platforms spanned both European integrated device manufacturers and a fast-expanding Chinese foundry ecosystem. Infineon Technologies, headquartered in Munich and among the world's largest power-semiconductor companies, built out GaN-on-Si capacity for its CoolGaN product family — an effort serving automotive traction inverters, data-centre power supplies, and industrial motor drives. STMicroelectronics, the Franco-Italian IDM, similarly expanded GaN epitaxy capacity as it pursued market position in 600V and 650V GaN device families. Both companies are established AIXTRON accounts whose capital programmes tracked the broader automotive-electrification and data-centre-power cycles.

Further up the risk curve, fabless and fab-lite GaN specialists — Navitas Semiconductor, EPC (Efficient Power Conversion), Power Integrations — represent a class of customer whose own growth depends on contracted wafer supply from GaN foundries that themselves run AIXTRON tools. GaN Systems, the Ottawa-based pure-play GaN power designer, was acquired by Infineon in 2023, consolidating engineering talent and capital-expenditure decision-making into a larger pool that remained aligned with the AIXTRON platform.

The most consequential new GaN customer geography, however, was China. Innoscience, a Zhuhai-based GaN-on-Si foundry backed by significant state-adjacent capital, emerged through 2022–2024 as one of the most aggressive capacity builders in the global GaN foundry landscape. The company's buildout of 8-inch GaN-on-Si capacity explicitly targeted consumer fast-charging, photovoltaic inverters, and data-centre power conversion — a ramp that translated into meaningful AIXTRON equipment orders. China's broader policy emphasis on domestic semiconductor self-sufficiency gave a structural tailwind to this activity that showed little sign of abating through the frozen snapshot window, even as export-control scrutiny across the wider semiconductor supply chain intensified.

AIXTRON's annual report and investor communications confirmed that power electronics — principally GaN — had become the single largest revenue contributor in the equipment mix by the mid-2020s, having displaced LED MOCVD tools as the dominant product line during the prior cycle.

## SiC Power Epitaxy: Entering a Contested Landscape

The G10-SiC platform, commercialised through 2023–2024, brought AIXTRON into direct competition with established SiC epi-tool suppliers including Veeco Instruments, as well as with purpose-built SiC specialists that had historically dominated silicon-carbide homoepitaxial growth. The SiC power device market itself was expanding rapidly, driven by EV traction inverter adoption — Tesla, BYD, and the European automotive OEM supply chains had collectively pulled forward enormous SiC demand — and Wolfspeed, the Cree spin-off, stood as the most prominent customer archetype: a vertically integrated SiC device maker racing to bring its Siler City, North Carolina mega-fab into full production.

STMicroelectronics appeared on both sides of the relevant customer map — it is among the world's largest SiC device makers and had disclosed capital-expenditure commitments running into the billions of dollars for SiC wafer and epi capacity expansion through 2027–2028. Whether AIXTRON's G10-SiC platform captured meaningful share of that spend was, at the snapshot date, only partly disclosed; the company acknowledged customer qualification processes and initial shipments but had not publicly named specific SiC accounts with the granularity it applied to its GaN customer relationships.

## Photonics: Datacom Lasers, VCSELs, and the Apple Tier-1 Supply Chain

AIXTRON's GaAs and InP MOCVD platforms — the older, more mature portion of the business — continued to serve the photonics supply chain with equipment for laser diodes, VCSELs, and high-electron-mobility transistor structures. Coherent Corp (formed by the 2022 combination of II-VI Incorporated and the legacy Coherent), Lumentum Holdings, Sumitomo Electric Industries, and Mitsubishi Electric represented the principal tier-1 device makers in this segment.

The VCSEL sub-segment commanded sustained attention because of its centrality to 3D sensing — specifically in the structured-light and time-of-flight proximity systems deployed in premium smartphones. Apple's Face ID module, which draws VCSELs sourced through tier-1 suppliers including Lumentum and II-VI/Coherent, became an indirect demand signal for AIXTRON tools, since those suppliers' capacity expansions required MOCVD epi platforms. Apple does not appear on any AIXTRON customer list directly; the relationship is architecturally buried two or three supply-chain tiers deep, visible in aggregate capital-expenditure flows rather than named accounts.

Automotive LiDAR added a second photonics growth vector. The expansion of production-intent LiDAR systems across the automotive OEM supply chain — through suppliers including Luminar, Innoviz, and Valeo — drove demand for pulsed-laser-diode and VCSEL capacity that fed back to the same tier-1 photonics device makers running AIXTRON tools.

## Micro-LED Display: The Thesis That Stalled

Micro-LED display generated substantial investor discussion but delivered minimal confirmed production-scale revenue. Apple's reported programme cancellation in early 2024 reset timeline expectations. Research tools and pilot-line equipment were in the field, but mass-production capacity orders had not materialised.

## Geographic Mix and Export-Control Exposure

AIXTRON's revenue has historically carried a pronounced Asian weighting, with China, Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan collectively accounting for the majority of equipment deliveries in most fiscal years. China alone, at peak LED MOCVD cycle volumes in the 2010s, exceeded half of group revenue in certain periods. Through the GaN power cycle of 2022–2024, China remained the single largest country revenue contributor — driven by Innoscience and the broader domestic GaN foundry buildout — though the proportional share moderated as European and North American GaN capacity orders grew.

| Region | Principal customer types | Demand driver |
|--------|--------------------------|---------------|
| China | GaN foundries (Innoscience et al.) | Domestic semi policy, consumer/solar power |
| Taiwan | Display, photonics | Micro-LED pilots, VCSEL |
| South Korea | Display OEMs | Micro-LED R&D |
| Japan | Photonics (Sumitomo, Mitsubishi) | Datacom, automotive LiDAR |
| North America | Wolfspeed (SiC), Navitas, EPC | EV, data centre |
| Europe | Infineon, STMicro | Automotive, industrial |

This China exposure drew sustained attention from AIXTRON's investor base and from German and European regulators. MOCVD equipment did not fall, through the snapshot date, within the most tightly controlled categories of the U.S. Commerce Department's Export Administration Regulations as applied to advanced logic and memory fabs. But compound-semiconductor epi tools occupy a grey zone in dual-use export control frameworks. AIXTRON applied for and received export licences on a transaction-by-transaction basis for sensitive end-users, disclosing compliance costs without quantifying lost-order exposure from licence denials. The October 2023 and subsequent expansions of U.S. advanced-chip export controls created a durable overhang: AIXTRON's GaN and SiC tools served power and photonics applications that remained outside the most stringent controls as of the snapshot date, but the regulatory trajectory pointed toward progressive tightening. Any future extension of compound-semiconductor controls into the GaN power device supply chain would directly affect Innoscience and comparable Chinese foundry customers.

## The Herzogenrath Footprint

AIXTRON operates a capital-light, design-and-assemble model from Herzogenrath. Critical components — quartz and ceramic reactor parts, gas delivery systems, vacuum hardware — are sourced from a global tier-one supplier base. The company expanded cleanroom test and assembly capacity during the 2022–2024 GaN power ramp. A smaller R&D facility in Abingdon, Oxfordshire supplements the German base.

chapters.title: Where AIXTRON sits against Veeco plus the broader MOCVD and compound-semi equipment set
chapters.body:
## The Duopoly That Survived the LED Bust

The global MOCVD market resolved into an effective duopoly: AIXTRON and Veeco Instruments together commanded roughly 80–90 percent of tool revenue at peak. Both refocused on power electronics and photonics while Chinese state-backed equipment makers absorbed the commodity LED segment.

## The Veeco Rivalry: From LED Wars to Power Electronics

Veeco Instruments (NASDAQ: VECO), headquartered in Plainview, New York, is AIXTRON's most direct competitor. Both peaked above €700m/$500m during the 2009–2012 LED boom, then contracted sharply. Veeco diversified via the $769m Ultratech acquisition in 2017; AIXTRON remained narrowly focused on MOCVD — a focus vindicated by the post-2020 compound-semiconductor transition. By 2023, both reported ~€629m/$600m in revenue, though Veeco's mix had shifted toward Ion Beam technology.

## Platform Comparison: G10-GaN versus Propel

The sharpest competitive battleground through 2023–2025 was GaN-on-Si epitaxy for power-electronics applications—the transistors and diodes going into data-centre power supplies, electric-vehicle chargers, and consumer adapters. AIXTRON's answer was the G10-GaN, a large-footprint planetary reactor offering high throughput for 150mm and 200mm GaN-on-Si wafers. Veeco's competitive tool was the Propel platform, a cluster architecture designed to deliver tight uniformity at volume.

The architectural difference was not cosmetic. AIXTRON's planetary-reactor heritage, inherited from the LED era, spread multiple wafers across a rotating susceptor, prioritising throughput in a production context. Veeco's Propel adopted a different geometry that its engineers argued delivered superior within-wafer uniformity—a claim resonating with customers targeting tight threshold-voltage distributions in power devices. The practical result was segmented adoption: AIXTRON tended to win at higher-volume commodity power customers, particularly across East Asia; Veeco had success with customers demanding the tightest specifications for automotive and data-centre power.

| Feature | AIXTRON G10-GaN | Veeco Propel GaN |
|---|---|---|
| Reactor architecture | Multi-wafer planetary (batch) | Cluster, single-run geometry |
| Target wafer sizes | 150 mm / 200 mm GaN-on-Si | 150 mm / 200 mm GaN-on-Si |
| Throughput profile | High batch throughput | Flexibility and uniformity emphasis |
| Geographic strength | Asia-Pacific, European Tier 1s | North America, diversified |
| SiC epi sibling | G10-SiC | Lumina SiC |

For SiC epitaxy—a newer battleground as the power-device industry expanded SiC adoption for EV inverters—the rivalry replicated itself at the platform level. AIXTRON's G10-SiC entered commercial qualification in the 2023–2025 period against Veeco's Lumina SiC platform and the established presence of LPE (Laboratorio di Progettazione Elettronico), the Milan-based specialist that had supplied SiC epi reactors to Wolfspeed and STMicroelectronics before AIXTRON entered the market. Applied Materials also held presence in SiC epitaxy CVD equipment, bringing a balance-sheet scale and customer-integration reach that neither AIXTRON nor Veeco could easily match. AIXTRON's G10-SiC entry was credible but late into a segment where LPE and Applied Materials already held qualification reference sites.

## Chinese MOCVD: A Contained but Funded Threat

The most visible competitive shift of the post-LED decade was the rise of Chinese domestic MOCVD equipment makers. Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment China (AMEC, 中微公司), listed on Shanghai's STAR Market, became China's flagship plasma-etch equipment supplier—but its MOCVD capabilities remained a secondary business line through 2025, more relevant for LED-era applications than for the high-specification compound-semiconductor work where AIXTRON competes. NAURA Technology Group (北方华创), a broader semiconductor equipment conglomerate, similarly maintained MOCVD tools in its portfolio alongside etch, furnace, and PVD equipment, but its MOCVD franchise did not penetrate the advanced power and photonics segments in a meaningful way before the frozen snapshot date.

What Chinese equipment makers did accomplish was the wholesale displacement of AIXTRON and Veeco from the commodity LED MOCVD market inside China. By the early 2020s, leading domestic LED producers—Sanan Optoelectronics, Huacan, and others—were procuring Chinese tools at lower price points for marginal capacity additions. AIXTRON effectively conceded that segment and did not contest it at low margin.

The more consequential question, unresolved as of May 2026, was whether AMEC, NAURA, or newer entrants could qualify for GaN power or SiC epi applications at the specification levels demanded by automotive Tier 1 suppliers. The answer, so far, was no—but the trajectory warranted monitoring. Chinese government industrial policy made compound-semiconductor self-sufficiency an explicit objective. The capability gap was real; so was the capital flowing toward closing it.

## Photonics: Niche Depth as a Defensive Moat

In photonics-grade MOCVD—InP-based laser diodes for datacom transceivers, GaAs VCSELs for 3D sensing, and tools for photonic integrated circuits—AIXTRON occupied territory where the competitive set narrowed considerably. Veeco retained a presence in photonics MOCVD, but the research and low-volume tiers were served by smaller specialists: Agnitron Technology in the United States and Thomas Swan in Cambridge—both research-tool vendors lacking the production scale to threaten AIXTRON's volume relationships with II-VI/Coherent, Lumentum, Sumitomo Electric, and Mitsubishi Electric.

The photonics segment mattered strategically because it provided revenue diversity that partially cushioned the cyclicality of the power-electronics capex cycle. Datacom laser orders—driven by hyperscaler data-centre build-out and AI-related optical-interconnect demand—sustained photonics MOCVD bookings through periods when power-device capex softened. Grawert signalled in commentary around the 2024 results period that photonics remained a structurally resilient portion of the order pipeline even as micro-LED uncertainty weighed on headline intake.

## Strategic Position: Structural Advantages and Exposed Flanks

AIXTRON's competitive position as of the frozen date rested on several structural advantages unlikely to erode quickly. European regulatory and customer relationships in automotive-grade qualification cycles—Infineon, STMicroelectronics, Bosch—favoured suppliers with established process history and local engineering support. AIXTRON's Herzogenrath base and German engineering culture aligned with Tier 1 automotive supply-chain norms in ways that a US or Chinese competitor found difficult to replicate through price alone. The G10 platform architecture, refined across multiple compound-semiconductor applications from GaN-on-Si to SiC to photonics, gave AIXTRON process-engineering depth that Chinese challengers had not yet replicated for power-grade applications. And the installed base of tools already operating at customer fabs—generating spares, process licenses, and upgrade revenue—provided a financial floor that new entrants could not access quickly.

The vulnerabilities were equally legible. The micro-LED display thesis deflated sharply after the Apple Watch programme cancellation reports in early 2024, removing an order catalyst that had been partially priced into expectations. The GaN power inventory digestion cycle of 2024 compounded the order-intake pressure, leaving AIXTRON navigating a simultaneous pause in two of its highest-growth vectors.

Chinese equipment makers' funded ambition to close the specification gap in power MOCVD remained a long-duration risk, even if it was not yet a near-term revenue threat. And Veeco—a well-capitalised competitor with its own platform evolution roadmap and a broader revenue base to sustain R&D through downturns—retained the capacity to win at premium specification nodes if its Propel architecture continued to demonstrate uniformity advantages at 200mm.

The duopoly that emerged from the LED era survived into the power-electronics transition. But it operated on more contested, application-specific terrain than the uniform LED-chipmaker capex cycle had once provided—and AIXTRON's ability to hold its position in each sub-segment rested on engineering reputation that required constant replenishment.

chapters.title: Timeline from 1983 founding through GaN power inflection and micro-LED reset
chapters.body:
## From the Aachen Laboratory to the GaN Inflection

AIXTRON listed on Frankfurt in 1998, joining what would become the SDAX. For its first two decades it occupied a narrow specialist position supplying MOCVD equipment for GaAs and InP devices. The defining commercial event of the company's first thirty years was in lighting.

## The LED Cycle: Boom, Bust, and Strategic Reset

Between 2008 and 2012, LED lighting drove AIXTRON's most explosive growth phase — revenue peaked as orders poured in from Asian and European device makers. The correction from 2012 was severe: Chinese subsidies underwrote domestic LED reactor procurement, and utilisation rates collapsed. Revenue contracted substantially through 2013–2014.

## The 2016 Interruption: Chinese Bid and the Forced Pivot

In 2016, FuJian Grand Chip Investment Fund GmbH made a takeover bid that was blocked by the United States on national security grounds under CFIUS review. The outcome reinforced the imperative to diversify into higher-value, defence-adjacent compound-semiconductor applications.

## The Grawert Era: Restructuring the Product Portfolio

Grawert presided over the product portfolio's most consequential reshaping, identifying three growth vectors: GaN power electronics, SiC power device epitaxy, and photonics. The G5 and G10 platforms became the commercial articulation. By 2023 the G10-GaN shipment ramp had become the principal revenue driver. At year-end 2023, Schulte retired and Grawert became sole CEO.

## The SiC Entry and the Micro-LED Reset

The G10-SiC platform, commercialised through 2023–2024, positioned AIXTRON in the SiC power epitaxy segment as a challenger. Simultaneously, the micro-LED thesis suffered a setback: Apple's reported programme cancellation removed a near-term demand catalyst.

## Forward Catalysts Through the 2026 Horizon

The compound-semiconductor capital cycle that frames AIXTRON's forward earnings trajectory rests on several concurrent adoption curves. GaN power electronics continued to penetrate automotive onboard chargers, data centre switched-mode power supplies, and industrial motor drives through 2025, with the pace of qualification wins at tier-one automotive OEM suppliers and hyperscaler power infrastructure providers setting the near-term order cadence for G10-GaN reactors. SiC epitaxy demand remained structurally tied to electric vehicle production volumes and the speed at which incumbent SiC device makers expanded wafer capacity, a trajectory subject to inventory correction dynamics that surfaced across the power semiconductor supply chain in 2024. Photonics represented the third demand vector: laser diode and VCSEL tool demand from datacom transceiver manufacturers — themselves supplying the AI infrastructure buildout that defined data centre capital expenditure through 2025 — provided a near-term counterweight to the micro-LED softness. Micro-LED display remained the long-duration option: a genuinely large total addressable market if the display-grade yield and cost curve could be solved, with the timeline no longer anchored to a single consumer product launch.

chapters.title: MOCVD reactor IP, compound-semi process technology, R&D framework
chapters.body:
## Planetary Reactors and the Aachen Inheritance

AIXTRON's intellectual identity was forged on a conviction: compound-semiconductor thin-film deposition required fundamentally better reactor geometry, not merely better chemistry.

The core of AIXTRON's IP estate is the **Planetary Reactor** concept — a design in which individual wafer carriers, called satellites, rotate on their own axes while simultaneously orbiting a central axis on a large rotating susceptor. The compound motion is not decorative engineering; it is the mechanism that exposes each wafer to the same time-averaged gas composition and thermal environment. In metal-organic chemical vapor deposition, where epitaxial layer thicknesses are measured in nanometres and dopant concentrations must be controlled to parts per billion, uniformity is not a specification category but a yield-determining variable. AIXTRON's patent filings, accumulated across four decades, reflect an obsessive refinement of this central geometry — satellite design, gas-foil rotation (which allows wafers to float on a thin cushion of process gas, reducing particle generation), susceptor materials, and the thermal boundary conditions that govern growth kinetics.

Alongside the Planetary Reactor family, AIXTRON developed the **Close Coupled Showerhead (CCS)** architecture, used in its AIX 2600 G5 platform and adapted for several optoelectronic applications. In the CCS design, the gas distribution plate sits in close proximity to the wafer surface, minimising the mixing length and enabling sharper compositional transitions between epitaxial layers — critical for heterojunction structures in laser diodes, VCSELs, and high-electron-mobility transistors. The two architectures — planetary susceptor and close-coupled showerhead — constitute a product bifurcation that lets AIXTRON address different substrate sizes, chemistries, and wafer-count economics across its tool catalogue.

## Process IP Across Material Systems

Each compound-semiconductor material system presents its own set of thermodynamic and chemical obstacles, and AIXTRON's process IP is stratified accordingly.

For **GaN-on-Si** power devices, the central challenge is managing the 17% thermal expansion mismatch between gallium nitride and silicon. Growing a crack-free, low-defect GaN stack on a 200mm silicon wafer requires a precisely engineered series of interlayers — aluminium nitride nucleation layers, aluminium gallium nitride step-graded buffers — whose composition and thickness profiles are the subject of proprietary process recipes embedded in the G5+ and G10-GaN tools. AIXTRON sells these recipes as part of the process package, not merely the hardware, which is a meaningful differentiator: a customer operating an AIXTRON G10-GaN receives validated process windows developed over years of internal and customer co-development, reducing the time to qualified production yield.

For **SiC homoepitaxy**, the physics are different in kind. Silicon carbide grows at temperatures above 1,500°C — roughly twice the growth temperature for GaN — and the chemistry involves chlorinated precursors that are corrosive to conventional reactor components. The G10-SiC platform, commercialised by 2023, required AIXTRON to develop susceptor materials, liner designs, and gas injection systems tolerant of those conditions.
